claim: During apoptosis, caspases degrade 8 out of ~30 nucleoporins to irreversibly demolish the nuclear pore complex.
source: During apoptosis, caspases degrade 8 out of ~30 nucleoporins to irreversibly demolish the nuclear pore complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Ferrando-May et al., 2001; Kihlmark et al., 2001; Patre et al., 2006) in the introduction.

claim: Sublethal activation of caspases during myogenesis results in the transient proteolysis of four peripheral Nups and one transmembrane Nup.
source: Here, we show that sublethal activation of caspases during myogenesis results in the transient proteolysis of four peripheral Nups and one transmembrane Nup.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Trimmed NPCs become nuclear export-defective.
source: 'Trimmed' NPCs become nuclear export-defective, and we identified in an unbiased manner several classes of cytoplasmic, plasma membrane, and mitochondrial proteins that rapidly accumulate in the nucleus.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NES-GFP reporter assays (Figure 1D-E) and mRNA export measurements (Figure 1C).

claim: Several classes of cytoplasmic, plasma membrane, and mitochondrial proteins rapidly accumulate in the nucleus during NPC trimming.
source: 'Trimmed' NPCs become nuclear export-defective, and we identified in an unbiased manner several classes of cytoplasmic, plasma membrane, and mitochondrial proteins that rapidly accumulate in the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: NPC trimming by non-apoptotic caspases was observed in neurogenesis.
source: NPC trimming by non-apoptotic caspases was also observed in neurogenesis and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting of differentiating neural precursor cells shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NPC trimming by non-apoptotic caspases was observed in endoplasmic reticulum stress.
source: NPC trimming by non-apoptotic caspases was also observed in neurogenesis and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tunicamycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Caspases can reversibly modulate nuclear transport activity at sublethal levels.
source: Our results suggest that caspases can reversibly modulate nuclear transport activity, which allows them to function as agents of cell differentiation and adaptation at sublethal levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the transient nature of NPC trimming and the recovery of Nup levels shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Caspase-3 is transiently activated at sublethal levels in differentiating cells.
source: However, studies in the last two decades have demonstrated that it is transiently activated at sublethal levels in differentiating cells (Burgon and Megeney, 2018; Connolly et al., 2014; Ding et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Sublethal caspase activation has been described in myogenic, neuronal, osteogenic, and many other types of differentiation.
source: This phenomenon has been described in myogenic, neuronal, osteogenic, and many other types of differentiation.
evidence: This is stated based on established literature.

claim: A total of eight nucleoporins are degraded by caspase-3 during apoptosis: Nup358, Nup214, Nup96, Nup93, Nup153, Tpr, Nup50, and Pom121.
source: A total of eight nucleoporins (Nups), the NPC subunits, are degraded by this cysteine protease: two out of the eight Nups are on the cytoplasmic side of the NPC (Nup358 and Nup214), two form NPC scaffold (Nup96 and Nup93), three reside on the nucleoplasmic side (Nup153, Tpr, and Nup50), and one is a transmembrane protein (Pom121).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work (Ferrando-May et al., 2001; Kihlmark et al., 2001; Patre et al., 2006).

claim: All major NPC substructures are destroyed during apoptosis: cytoplasmic filaments, central scaffold, nuclear basket, and membrane-bound portion.
source: Hence, all major NPC substructures – cytoplasmic filaments, central scaffold, nuclear basket, and membrane-bound portion – are destroyed.
evidence: This is inferred from the identity and locations of the eight Nups degraded during apoptosis.

claim: Transient caspase-3 activation in differentiating myoblasts has been shown by immunoblotting and fluorogenic probes.
source: Transient caspase-3 activation in differentiating myoblasts has been shown by immunoblotting and fluorogenic probes.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work in the field.

claim: Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of caspase-3 significantly inhibits cell-cell fusion and expression of key muscle genes.
source: Moreover, genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of caspase-3 significantly inhibits cell-cell fusion and expression of key muscle genes.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: During myogenesis, caspase-3 molecularly 'trims' the NPC in a reversible manner rather than dismantling the entire structure as in apoptosis.
source: Here, we show that during myogenesis, caspase-3 molecularly 'trims' the NPC in a reversible manner rather than dismantling the entire structure as in apoptosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the selective degradation of peripheral Nups while scaffold Nups remain intact (Figure 1).

claim: Partial degradation of the NPC transiently impairs nuclear export, but not nuclear import and passive permeability barrier.
source: This partial degradation of the NPC transiently impairs nuclear export, but not nuclear import and passive permeability barrier, and accompanies nuclear accumulation of focal adhesion proteins, tubulins, Annexin A's, mitochondrial enzymes, etc.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NES-GFP assays (Figure 1D-E), dextran exclusion assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and importin localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: NPC trimming accompanies nuclear accumulation of focal adhesion proteins, tubulins, Annexin A's, and mitochondrial enzymes.
source: This partial degradation of the NPC transiently impairs nuclear export, but not nuclear import and passive permeability barrier, and accompanies nuclear accumulation of focal adhesion proteins, tubulins, Annexin A's, mitochondrial enzymes, etc.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting (Figure 1F-G) and mass spectrometry (Figures 3-4).

claim: NPC trimming explains how FAK becomes transiently nuclear, which is required for myogenin de-repression.
source: Of note, NPC trimming explains how FAK becomes transiently nuclear, which previously was shown to be required for myogenin de-repression (Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the nuclear accumulation of FAK during NPC trimming (Figure 1G) and prior work showing FAK's role in myogenin regulation.

claim: NPC trimming is observed in differentiating primary myoblasts.
source: NPC trimming is observed in differentiating primary myoblasts and neural precursor cells as well, illustrating that it may be a general feature of cell differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence of primary myoblasts shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NPC trimming is observed in differentiating neural precursor cells.
source: NPC trimming is observed in differentiating primary myoblasts and neural precursor cells as well, illustrating that it may be a general feature of cell differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting of differentiating neurons shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NPC trimming may be a general feature of cell differentiation.
source: NPC trimming is observed in differentiating primary myoblasts and neural precursor cells as well, illustrating that it may be a general feature of cell differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in multiple cell types (myoblasts and neurons).

claim: NPC trimming in ER-stressed cells suggests that caspase-mediated modulation of nuclear transport might represent a part of the cellular stress response system.
source: We also observed NPC trimming in ER-stressed cells, suggesting that caspase-mediated modulation of nuclear transport might represent not only a programmed step in differentiation but also a part of the cellular stress response system.
evidence: This is inferred from tunicamycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Caspase-3 can degrade eight Nups during staurosporine-, actinomycin D-, etoposide-, or TRAIL-induced apoptosis.
source: Caspase-3 can degrade eight Nups (Nup358, Nup214, Nup153, Nup96, Nup93, Nup50, Tpr, and Pom121) during staurosporine-, actinomycin D-, etoposide-, or TRAIL-induced apoptosis (Ferrando-May et al., 2001; Patre et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Recombinant caspase-3 reproduces in vivo Nup fragmentation pattern when added to permeabilized cells.
source: Recombinant caspase-3 reproduces in vivo Nup fragmentation pattern when added to permeabilized cells, and its pharmacological inhibition by DEVD-CHO blocks Nup degradation during apoptosis (Ferrando-May et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of caspase-3 by DEVD-CHO blocks Nup degradation during apoptosis.
source: Recombinant caspase-3 reproduces in vivo Nup fragmentation pattern when added to permeabilized cells, and its pharmacological inhibition by DEVD-CHO blocks Nup degradation during apoptosis (Ferrando-May et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Nups were identified as caspase-3 targets in multiple substrate profiling experiments.
source: Nups were identified as caspase-3 targets in multiple substrate profiling experiments as well (https://wellslab.ucsf.edu/degrabase/).
evidence: This is stated based on database information.

claim: Nup358 is cleaved at 8+ sites by caspase-3.
source: Rendering them caspase-3-resistant is technically not feasible as most of them are cleaved at multiple sites – for example, 8+for Nup358 and 4+for Tpr (Patre et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Tpr is cleaved at 4+ sites by caspase-3.
source: Rendering them caspase-3-resistant is technically not feasible as most of them are cleaved at multiple sites – for example, 8+for Nup358 and 4+for Tpr (Patre et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Nup153 is cleaved at 6+ sites by caspase-3.
source: We observe 6+fragments for Nup153 (see below).
evidence: This is observed in the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Human Pom121 has been made uncleavable by D531A mutation.
source: However, human Pom121 has been made uncleavable by D531A mutation (Kihlmark et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: The active form of caspase-3 was detected in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: As reported previously, we detected the active form of caspase-3 as well as that of caspase-9 and –12 in differentiating C2C12 cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Fernando et al., 2002; Gomez-Cavazos and Hetzer, 2015; Murray et al., 2008; Nakanishi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The active form of caspase-9 was detected in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: As reported previously, we detected the active form of caspase-3 as well as that of caspase-9 and –12 in differentiating C2C12 cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Fernando et al., 2002; Gomez-Cavazos and Hetzer, 2015; Murray et al., 2008; Nakanishi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The active form of caspase-12 was detected in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: As reported previously, we detected the active form of caspase-3 as well as that of caspase-9 and –12 in differentiating C2C12 cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Fernando et al., 2002; Gomez-Cavazos and Hetzer, 2015; Murray et al., 2008; Nakanishi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Caspase activity peaks at 16–24 hr after inducing myogenesis.
source: Typically, caspase activity peaks at 16–24 hr after inducing myogenesis, and is fully quenched by 32–60 hr (see Cell culture in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is observed in the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Caspase activity is fully quenched by 32–60 hr after inducing myogenesis.
source: Typically, caspase activity peaks at 16–24 hr after inducing myogenesis, and is fully quenched by 32–60 hr (see Cell culture in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is observed in the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Peak caspase-3 activity level in differentiating C2C12 cells is comparable to that in C2C12 cells treated with 1 μM staurosporine for 4 hr.
source: As a reference, peak caspase-3 activity level in differentiating C2C12 cells is comparable to that in C2C12 cells treated with 1 μM staurosporine for 4 hr (Murray et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Four peripheral Nups (Nup358, Nup214, Nup153, and Tpr) were reversibly and completely degraded in a caspase-dependent manner during myogenesis.
source: During this time window, 4 peripheral Nups, Nup358, Nup214, Nup153, and Tpr, were reversibly and completely degraded in a caspase-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting with and without caspase inhibitor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Complete loss of full-length Nups demonstrates that proteolysis takes place in the differentiating population, not just in 2–3% of the population that undergo apoptosis during C2C12 myogenesis.
source: Complete loss of full-length proteins demonstrates that this proteolytic event takes place in the differentiating population, not just in 2–3% of the population that undergo apoptosis during C2C12 myogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the complete disappearance of full-length Nups in immunoblots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Nup50 was partially proteolyzed during myogenesis.
source: Although partially, Nup50 was proteolyzed as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nup96 remained intact during myogenesis.
source: Nup96 and Nup93, which form NPC scaffold and are cleaved during apoptosis (Patre et al., 2006), remained intact.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nup93 remained intact during myogenesis.
source: Nup96 and Nup93, which form NPC scaffold and are cleaved during apoptosis (Patre et al., 2006), remained intact.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1A, though a secondary band appears.

claim: The same Nup96 and Nup93 copies persist through the course of myogenesis.
source: This agrees with our previous report showing the persistence of the same Nup96 and Nup93 copies through the course of myogenesis (Toyama et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Calpain inhibition delayed but did not prevent caspase-3/12 activation and peripheral Nup degradation.
source: Interestingly, it delayed but did not prevent caspase-3/12 activation and peripheral Nup degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting with calpain inhibitor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Calpains participate in caspase activation process but are not responsible for NPC trimming.
source: This suggests that they participate in caspase activation process but are not responsible for NPC trimming.
evidence: This is inferred from the calpain inhibition experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Central FG Nups, such as Nup98 and Nup62, are not targeted by caspases.
source: Given that central FG Nups, such as Nup98 and Nup62, are not targeted by caspases (Ferrando-May et al., 2001; Patre et al., 2006), we surmised that the nuclear passive permeability barrier would remain intact.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: The nuclear passive permeability barrier remains functional even when the NPC is partially disintegrated.
source: Indeed, nuclear exclusion of ≥40 kDa dextrans demonstrates that the passive barrier is functional even when the NPC is partially disintegrated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dextran exclusion assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The removal of Nup358, Nup214, Nup153, or Tpr blocks nuclear export and causes nuclear accumulation of RNAs and NES-containing proteins.
source: The removal of Nup358, Nup214, Nup153, or Tpr has been shown to block nuclear export and cause nuclear accumulation of RNAs and NES (nuclear export signal)-containing proteins (Aksenova et al., 2020; Forler et al., 2004; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2006; Ullman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: The nuclear-to-total mRNA ratio increases from 34% to 60% during the first three days of myogenic differentiation.
source: The nuclear-to-total mRNA ratio increases from 34% to 60% during differentiation, indicating an impairment in mRNA export (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by poly(A)+ RNA quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increase in nuclear-to-total mRNA ratio during myogenic differentiation indicates an impairment in mRNA export.
source: The nuclear-to-total mRNA ratio increases from 34% to 60% during differentiation, indicating an impairment in mRNA export (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased nuclear retention of mRNA.

claim: The distribution of housekeeping gene RNAs (18 S rRNA and Gapdh transcript) remains unchanged during myogenic differentiation.
source: Of note, the distribution of housekeeping gene RNAs, 18 S rRNA and Gapdh transcript, remains unchanged during this period as they have extended half-lives (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C; Lee et al., 2010; Yi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA FISH shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Housekeeping gene RNAs have extended half-lives.
source: Of note, the distribution of housekeeping gene RNAs, 18 S rRNA and Gapdh transcript, remains unchanged during this period as they have extended half-lives (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C; Lee et al., 2010; Yi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Cells can continue to synthesize essential proteins and maintain homeostasis even when RNA export is temporarily inhibited.
source: This might explain how cells can continue to synthesize essential proteins and maintain homeostasis even when RNA export is temporarily inhibited.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that housekeeping RNAs remain stable.

claim: The cytoplasmic-to-nuclear ratio of NESRev-GFP was significantly lower in myoblasts undergoing cell-cell fusion than in myotubes.
source: The cytoplasmic-to-nuclear ratio of NESRev-GFP, a widely used export probe, was significantly lower in myoblasts undergoing cell-cell fusion than in myotubes (Figure 1D and E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging and quantification shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The cytoplasmic-to-nuclear ratio of NESPKI-GFP significantly decreased when myoblasts started to produce bubbling blebs and became fusion-competent.
source: Similarly, the cytoplasmic-to-nuclear ratio of NESPKI-GFP significantly decreased when myoblasts started to produce "bubbling" blebs and became fusion-competent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–G; Lian et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging and quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F-G.

claim: α-tubulin is normally absent in the nucleus due to the presence of multiple NESs.
source: We also asked if the localization of α-tubulin is affected. It is normally absent in the nucleus due to the presence of multiple NESs (Schwarzerová et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: α-tubulin was detected in the nuclear lysate 1 day post-differentiation when NPCs are partially disintegrated.
source: Strikingly, 1 day post-differentiation when NPCs are partially disintegrated, α-tubulin was detected in the nuclear lysate, although at a relatively low level (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting of nuclear fractions shown in Figure 1F.

claim: When NPC trimming was blocked by Q-VD-OPh, nuclear translocation of α-tubulin was suppressed.
source: When NPC trimming was blocked by Q-VD-OPh, a pan-caspase inhibitor, its nuclear translocation was suppressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting with caspase inhibitor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Focal adhesion proteins contain NESs.
source: We next checked if focal adhesion proteins behave similarly since they (1) contain NESs as well and (2) are likely to be released to the cytoplasm by calpains in differentiating C2C12 cells (Louis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on prior knowledge and literature.

claim: Focal adhesion proteins are likely to be released to the cytoplasm by calpains in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: We next checked if focal adhesion proteins behave similarly since they (1) contain NESs as well and (2) are likely to be released to the cytoplasm by calpains in differentiating C2C12 cells (Louis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: All four focal adhesion proteins examined (Hic-5, zyxin, paxillin, and FAK) became transiently nuclear during myogenesis.
source: Remarkably, all four focal adhesion proteins that we examined (Hic-5, zyxin, paxillin, and FAK) became transiently nuclear during myogenesis (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting of nuclear fractions shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In the presence of Q-VD-OPh, nuclear entrapment of focal adhesion proteins was notably suppressed, albeit not fully.
source: In the presence of Q-VD-OPh, their nuclear entrapment was notably suppressed, albeit not fully (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting with caspase inhibitor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The residual nuclear accumulation of focal adhesion proteins can be attributed to forced import during myogenesis by their binding partners that use them as transcription cofactors in the nucleus.
source: The residual amount can be attributed to forced import during myogenesis by their binding partners that make use of them as transcription cofactors in the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial suppression by caspase inhibitor and known roles of these proteins.

claim: Interaction between FAK and MBD2 was detected by proximity ligation assay.
source: We indeed detect interaction between FAK and MBD2 (Luo et al., 2009) and Hic-5 and androgen receptor (Alpha et al., 2020) by proximity ligation assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Interaction between Hic-5 and androgen receptor was detected by proximity ligation assay.
source: We indeed detect interaction between FAK and MBD2 (Luo et al., 2009) and Hic-5 and androgen receptor (Alpha et al., 2020) by proximity ligation assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Differentiation-associated caspase activity impairs nuclear export and leads to the nuclear retention of NES-containing proteins.
source: In summary, differentiation-associated caspase activity impairs nuclear export and leads to the nuclear retention of NES-containing proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple experiments showing nuclear accumulation of NES-containing proteins.

claim: Leptomycin B, a Crm1 inhibitor, could support myogenesis.
source: Given the rapid influx of NES-harboring proteins, we hypothesized that leptomycin B, a Crm1 inhibitor, could support myogenesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that NPC trimming impairs nuclear export.

claim: When differentiation medium is supplemented with a partial dose of leptomycin B, myogenin expression is enhanced.
source: Indeed, when differentiation medium is supplemented with a partial dose of leptomycin B, myogenin expression is enhanced (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: 6 hr of leptomycin B pre-treatment in growth medium results in ~twofold myogenin enhancement.
source: This agrees with the reported ~twofold myogenin enhancement by 6 hr of leptomycin B pre-treatment in growth medium (Bustos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: A full dose of Q-VD-OPh in differentiation medium significantly suppresses myogenin upregulation.
source: In contrast, a full dose of Q-VD-OPh in differentiation medium significantly suppresses myogenin upregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Q-VD-OPh significantly reduces cell-cell fusion and myosin heavy chain expression.
source: Q-VD-OPh significantly reduces cell-cell fusion and myosin heavy chain expression as well (Murray et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Only the C-terminal epitope of Tpr dissociates from the NPC in late-stage apoptotic nuclei.
source: Immunostaining revealed that only the C-terminal epitope of Tpr dissociates from the NPC while proteolyzed Nup153 and Tpr N-terminus remain bound (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Proteolyzed Nup153 remains bound to the NPC in late-stage apoptotic nuclei.
source: Immunostaining revealed that only the C-terminal epitope of Tpr dissociates from the NPC while proteolyzed Nup153 and Tpr N-terminus remain bound (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Tpr N-terminus remains bound to the NPC in late-stage apoptotic nuclei.
source: Immunostaining revealed that only the C-terminal epitope of Tpr dissociates from the NPC while proteolyzed Nup153 and Tpr N-terminus remain bound (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The persistent association of proteolyzed Nup153 and Tpr with the NPC is reminiscent of that of enterovirus 2 A or rhinovirus 3 C protease-cleaved Nup98.
source: Their persistent association with the NPC is reminiscent of that of enterovirus 2 A or rhinovirus 3 C protease-cleaved Nup98 (Park et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work on viral protease-cleaved Nups.

claim: Tpr C-terminal fragment dissociates partially in differentiating myoblasts.
source: Differentiating myoblasts exhibited a proteolytic phenotype that is distinct from that of apoptotic cells. Quantitative analysis suggests that Tpr C-terminal fragment dissociates partially (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Only in 5–10% of differentiating cells was the Tpr C-terminal fragment completely dissociated as in apoptotic cells.
source: Only in 5–10% of the cells were the fragment completely dissociated as in apoptotic cells (dotted boxes in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed in immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TprC– population can be clearly distinguished from dying cells by nuclear morphology.
source: 'TprC–' population can be clearly distinguished from dying cells by nuclear morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The nucleoplasmic pool of Crm1 is lost and it becomes confined to the nuclear periphery in apoptotic cells.
source: Moreover, while the nucleoplasmic pool of Crm1 is lost and it becomes confined to the nuclear periphery in apoptotic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), Crm1 localization did not change in differentiating cells, even in TprC– cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Crm1 localization did not change in differentiating cells, even in TprC– cells.
source: Moreover, while the nucleoplasmic pool of Crm1 is lost and it becomes confined to the nuclear periphery in apoptotic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), Crm1 localization did not change in differentiating cells, even in TprC– cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NPC trimming results in a subdued nuclear export defect compared to a full dose of leptomycin B.
source: This might explain why NPC trimming results in a subdued nuclear export defect compared to a full dose of leptomycin B; NES-containing focal adhesion proteins accumulate in the nucleus to a limited extent during NPC trimming (Figure 1G) but become predominantly nuclear upon leptomycin B treatment (Nix et al., 2001; Ossovskaya et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Crm1 localization and the extent of nuclear accumulation of focal adhesion proteins.

claim: NES-containing focal adhesion proteins become predominantly nuclear upon leptomycin B treatment.
source: This might explain why NPC trimming results in a subdued nuclear export defect compared to a full dose of leptomycin B; NES-containing focal adhesion proteins accumulate in the nucleus to a limited extent during NPC trimming (Figure 1G) but become predominantly nuclear upon leptomycin B treatment (Nix et al., 2001; Ossovskaya et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Nup153 fragments were found exclusively in the nuclear insoluble fraction.
source: Nup153 fragments were found exclusively in the former.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting of nuclear subfractions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The C-terminal piece of Tpr is expected to be ~37 kDa.
source: In contrast, the C-terminal piece of Tpr, which is expected to be ~37 kDa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Ferrando-May et al., 2001), was detected in both subfractions.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work and domain architecture.

claim: The C-terminal piece of Tpr was detected in both nuclear insoluble and nuclear soluble subfractions.
source: In contrast, the C-terminal piece of Tpr, which is expected to be ~37 kDa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Ferrando-May et al., 2001), was detected in both subfractions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting of nuclear subfractions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Pom121 has a short transmembrane domain (aminoacid 35–55 in human) and a long pore-side domain (aminoacid 56–1249 in human).
source: Pom121 has a short transmembrane and a long pore-side domain (aminoacid 35–55 and 56–1249 respectively in human; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated based on known protein structure.

claim: The pore-side domain of Pom121 is caspase-cleaved and is undetectable by immunostaining in apoptotic cells.
source: The latter is caspase-cleaved and is undetectable by immunostaining in apoptotic cells (Kihlmark et al., 2001; Kihlmark et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Pom121 is proteolyzed to completion at 24 hr post-differentiation.
source: Although Pom121 is proteolyzed to completion at 24 hr post-differentiation (Figure 1B), immunostaining shows that its pore side domain does not fully dissociate from the NPC (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The pore-side domain of Pom121 does not fully dissociate from the NPC during myogenesis.
source: Although Pom121 is proteolyzed to completion at 24 hr post-differentiation (Figure 1B), immunostaining shows that its pore side domain does not fully dissociate from the NPC (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: There is heterogeneity in the behavior of caspase-generated Nup fragments.
source: To conclude, there is some heterogeneity in the behavior of caspase-generated Nup fragments while NES-GFP reporter demonstrates that most, if not all, NPCs become export-defective.
evidence: This is concluded from the observations of partial dissociation of Tpr and Pom121 fragments.

claim: NES-GFP reporter demonstrates that most, if not all, NPCs become export-defective during myogenesis.
source: To conclude, there is some heterogeneity in the behavior of caspase-generated Nup fragments while NES-GFP reporter demonstrates that most, if not all, NPCs become export-defective.
evidence: This is inferred from the NES-GFP reporter data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Trimmed NPCs do not cluster like they do in late-stage apoptosis.
source: Lastly, we confirmed that trimmed NPCs do not cluster like they do in late-stage apoptosis via maximum intensity Z projection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Kihlmark et al., 2001), and that the localization of importins is unaffected by NPC trimming (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by maximum intensity Z projection imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The localization of importins is unaffected by NPC trimming.
source: Lastly, we confirmed that trimmed NPCs do not cluster like they do in late-stage apoptosis via maximum intensity Z projection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Kihlmark et al., 2001), and that the localization of importins is unaffected by NPC trimming (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry was used to study how NPC trimming affects the nuclear proteome.
source: Next, we employed quantitative mass spectrometry to study how NPC trimming affects the nuclear proteome.
evidence: This is the method described for the experiments shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: All focal adhesion proteins but tensins became significantly more nuclear during myogenesis.

claim: Several α/β-tubulin isoforms and microtubule regulators displayed nuclear accumulation during myogenesis.
source: Several α/β-tubulin isoforms and microtubule regulators displayed similar behavior.

claim: Tppp3 (Tubulin polymerization promoting protein family member 3) was the top hit in the tubulin/microtubule regulator group.

claim: The nuclear level of S100a10, an Annexin A2 interactor, increased sharply during myogenesis.

claim: Several mitochondrial enzymes accumulate in the nucleus during myogenesis.

claim: A subset of the Krebs cycle enzymes has been reported to enter the nucleus during embryogenesis.
source: A subset of the Krebs cycle enzymes has been reported to enter the nucleus during embryogenesis (Nagaraj et al., 2017), and we find the same in myogenic differentiation.

claim: A subset of the Krebs cycle enzymes enter the nucleus during myogenic differentiation.
source: A subset of the Krebs cycle enzymes has been reported to enter the nucleus during embryogenesis (Nagaraj et al., 2017), and we find the same in myogenic differentiation.

claim: The nuclear levels of most E3 ligases and proteasome subunits remain relatively stable during myogenesis.
source: Lastly, the nuclear levels of most E3 ligases and proteasome subunits remain relatively stable, but there were a few exceptions such as Itch, Ufl1, Psme1, and Psmb3.

source: Lastly, the nuclear levels of most E3 ligases and proteasome subunits remain relatively stable, but there were a few exceptions such as Itch, Ufl1, Psme1, and Psmb3.

claim: Enhanced synthesis is a major factor in increasing nuclear protein levels during myogenesis.
source: Our color-mapped volcano plot shows that most transcriptionally upregulated proteins (red data points in Figure 3C and D) become more abundant in the nucleus, demonstrating that enhanced synthesis is another major factor.

claim: Out of 700 proteins that show >twofold increase in the nuclear level during the first 24 hr, all but four display less increase when caspases are inhibited.
source: Out of 700 proteins that show >twofold increase in the nuclear level during the first 24 hr (area shaded in red in Figure 4B), all but four display less increase when caspases are inhibited.

claim: NPC trimming plays a key role in shaping the nuclear proteome during myogenesis.
source: This is in line with our view that NPC trimming plays a key role in shaping the nuclear proteome (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that caspase inhibition reduces nuclear accumulation of most proteins.

claim: The nuclear proteome changes dramatically and rapidly in response to the myogenic signal.
source: In sum, our data (1) illustrates that the nuclear proteome changes dramatically and rapidly in response to the myogenic signal, (2) reveals the importance of protein translocation in cell differentiation, and (3) provides a fresh list of proteins that have been overlooked in the context of myotube formation.

claim: Protein translocation is important in cell differentiation.
source: In sum, our data (1) illustrates that the nuclear proteome changes dramatically and rapidly in response to the myogenic signal, (2) reveals the importance of protein translocation in cell differentiation, and (3) provides a fresh list of proteins that have been overlooked in the context of myotube formation.

claim: Survivin downregulation precedes caspase-3 activation in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: In differentiating C2C12 cells, survivin downregulation precedes caspase-3 activation, indicating that the latter occurs after the very last cell division and as cells enter G0 (Figure 5B).

claim: Caspase-3 activation occurs after the very last cell division and as cells enter G0.
source: In differentiating C2C12 cells, survivin downregulation precedes caspase-3 activation, indicating that the latter occurs after the very last cell division and as cells enter G0 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of survivin downregulation and caspase-3 activation.

claim: Active caspase-3 arises before myogenin during myogenesis.
source: We then determined the timing of caspase-3 activation relative to the upregulation of myogenin, which marks the point-of-no-return. Both immunoblotting and immunstaining show that active caspase-3 arises before myogenin (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells can remain NPC-trimmed for a brief period after myogenin upregulation.
source: Interestingly, cells can remain NPC-trimmed for a brief period after myogenin upregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of TprC– Myog+ cells.

claim: TprC– Myog– cells were identified in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: We not only identified TprC– Myog– but also TprC– Myog+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: TprC– Myog+ cells were identified in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: We not only identified TprC– Myog– but also TprC– Myog+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The presence of TprC– Myog+ cells signifies that nuclear import is functional even when NPCs are trimmed.
source: The presence of the latter signifies that nuclear import is functional even when NPCs are trimmed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that myogenin, which must be imported, is present in TprC– cells.

claim: TprC– Myog– and TprC– Myog+ cell states appear in differentiating primary myoblasts.
source: The same transitory cell states appear in differentiating primary myoblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that this is not a C2C12-specific phenomenon.

claim: Caspase-3 is quenched by the time myosin heavy chain is expressed.
source: Caspase-3 is quenched by the time myosin heavy chain is expressed, that is, when cell-cell fusion occurs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: When myogenesis is accelerated by GFP-myogenin overexpression, caspase-3 is quenched a day earlier compared to the control condition.
source: When myogenesis is accelerated by GFP-myogenin overexpression, caspase-3 is quenched a day earlier compared to the control condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), signifying that a caspase-quenching pathway exists and is activated once myoblasts pass a certain differentiation stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A caspase-quenching pathway exists and is activated once myoblasts pass a certain differentiation stage.
source: When myogenesis is accelerated by GFP-myogenin overexpression, caspase-3 is quenched a day earlier compared to the control condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), signifying that a caspase-quenching pathway exists and is activated once myoblasts pass a certain differentiation stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that caspase-3 quenching is accelerated when differentiation is accelerated.

claim: Survivin is highly expressed in G2/M phase but rapidly downregulated in early G1.
source: Survivin is a chromosomal passenger complex subunit that is highly expressed in G2/M phase but rapidly downregulated in early G1 (Li et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Survivin is highly expressed in neural precursor cells but undetectable in mature neurons.
source: As in myogenic differentiation, survivin is highly expressed in precursor cells but undetectable in mature neurons, and the activation of caspase-3 and the proteolysis of Nup153 and PARP occurred concomitantly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The activation of caspase-3 and the proteolysis of Nup153 and PARP occurred concomitantly during neuronal differentiation.
source: As in myogenic differentiation, survivin is highly expressed in precursor cells but undetectable in mature neurons, and the activation of caspase-3 and the proteolysis of Nup153 and PARP occurred concomitantly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Caspases play similar roles during neuronal differentiation as in myogenic differentiation, albeit over a longer duration.
source: This suggests that caspases play similar roles during neuronal differentiation, albeit over a longer duration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of NPC trimming in both myogenesis and neurogenesis.

claim: The calpain/caspase activation cascade in differentiating myoblasts is reminiscent of that in unfolded protein response.
source: Interestingly, however, the calpain/caspase activation cascade in differentiating myoblasts is reminiscent of that in unfolded protein response.
evidence: This is a comparison based on known signaling pathways.

claim: Active caspase-3 arose in both myotubes and reserve cells at comparable levels upon tunicamycin treatment.
source: Active caspase-3 arose in both cell types at comparable levels; however, in myotubes, Nup153 and Tpr were fully proteolyzed by 6 hours.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In myotubes treated with tunicamycin, Nup153 and Tpr were fully proteolyzed by 6 hours.
source: Active caspase-3 arose in both cell types at comparable levels; however, in myotubes, Nup153 and Tpr were fully proteolyzed by 6 hours.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The discrepancy in Nup proteolysis between myotubes and reserve cells can be attributed to XIAP.
source: The discrepancy can be attributed to XIAP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that XIAP levels are lower in myotubes.

claim: XIAP is the major caspase-inhibiting protein.
source: XIAP is the major caspase-inhibiting protein, and its level is significantly lower in myotubes at 0 hr.
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge.

claim: XIAP level is significantly lower in myotubes compared to reserve cells at 0 hr.
source: XIAP is the major caspase-inhibiting protein, and its level is significantly lower in myotubes at 0 hr.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5E.

claim: XIAP in myotubes migrates faster than that in reserve cells during gel electrophoresis, possibly due to Ser87 dephosphorylation.
source: (XIAP in myotubes migrates faster than that in reserve cells during gel electrophoresis, possibly due to Ser87 dephosphorylation, which stabilizes XIAP Kato et al., 2011.)
evidence: This is observed in the immunoblot shown in Figure 5E and explained based on prior work.

claim: Ser87 dephosphorylation stabilizes XIAP.
source: (XIAP in myotubes migrates faster than that in reserve cells during gel electrophoresis, possibly due to Ser87 dephosphorylation, which stabilizes XIAP Kato et al., 2011.)
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: NESRev-GFP becomes more nuclear in ER-stressed myotubes.
source: ER stress-induced NPC trimming exhibits multiple similarities to that during myogenesis: (1) NESRev-GFP becomes more nuclear (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), (2) 5–10% of myotubes become TprC– while retaining Nup153 epitopes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H), and (3) Nup93 remains unaffected, again illustrating that scaffold Nups are better protected from caspases (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 5–10% of ER-stressed myotubes become TprC– while retaining Nup153 epitopes.
source: ER stress-induced NPC trimming exhibits multiple similarities to that during myogenesis: (1) NESRev-GFP becomes more nuclear (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), (2) 5–10% of myotubes become TprC– while retaining Nup153 epitopes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H), and (3) Nup93 remains unaffected, again illustrating that scaffold Nups are better protected from caspases (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Nup93 remains unaffected during ER stress, illustrating that scaffold Nups are better protected from caspases.
source: ER stress-induced NPC trimming exhibits multiple similarities to that during myogenesis: (1) NESRev-GFP becomes more nuclear (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), (2) 5–10% of myotubes become TprC– while retaining Nup153 epitopes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H), and (3) Nup93 remains unaffected, again illustrating that scaffold Nups are better protected from caspases (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Low-level but sustained ER stress induces NPC trimming.
source: We maintained differentiated C2C12 cells at low doses of tunicamycin (<50 ng/mL) for a week (Figure 5F). As in differentiating myoblasts and acutely ER stressed-myotubes, the breakdown of Nup93 was minimal, whereas 4 peripheral Nups were noticeably degraded.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Chronic ER stress forces the NPC to remain in the trimmed form for a prolonged period before apoptosis is triggered.
source: In short, chronic ER stress forces the NPC to remain in the trimmed form for a prolonged period before apoptosis is triggered.
evidence: This is inferred from the sustained NPC trimming observed in chronic tunicamycin treatment shown in Figure 5F.

claim: During apoptosis, the NPC is completely demolished by fully activated caspase-3.
source: During apoptosis, the NPC is completely demolished by fully activated caspase-3.
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and prior work.

claim: In differentiating cells, caspase-3 activation is sublethal, and it selectively targets NPC projections.
source: In differentiating cells, caspase-3 activation is sublethal, and it selectively targets NPC projections, that is, cytoplasmic filaments, nuclear basket, and Pom121 pore-side domain (Figure 6).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarized in Figure 6.

claim: Caspase-mediated NPC trimming is a reversible process that transiently impairs nuclear export.
source: Caspase-mediated NPC trimming is a reversible process that transiently impairs nuclear export.
evidence: This is concluded from the transient nature of NPC trimming and the recovery of Nup levels.

claim: The phenotype of NPC trimming is somewhat reminiscent of that of cells exposed to picornavirus 2 A protease.
source: This phenotype is somewhat reminiscent of that of cells exposed to picornavirus 2 A protease, where Nup98 is selectively degraded from the NPC and mRNA/protein export is inhibited while nuclear import and passive permeability barrier remain mostly functional (Serganov et al., 2022).

claim: In cells exposed to picornavirus 2 A protease, Nup98 is selectively degraded from the NPC and mRNA/protein export is inhibited while nuclear import and passive permeability barrier remain mostly functional.
source: This phenotype is somewhat reminiscent of that of cells exposed to picornavirus 2 A protease, where Nup98 is selectively degraded from the NPC and mRNA/protein export is inhibited while nuclear import and passive permeability barrier remain mostly functional (Serganov et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: NPC trimming coincides with the nuclear influx/retention of non-nuclear proteins.
source: NPC trimming coincides with the nuclear influx/retention of non-nuclear proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: The nuclear level of FAK surges during myogenesis to remove MBD2 from methylated CpGs within the Myog promoter.
source: The nuclear level of FAK, a focal adhesion protein with both nuclear export and localization signals, was previously shown to surge during myogenesis to remove MBD2 – the main component of the gene-repressing NuRD (nucleosome remodeling and deacetylation) complex – from methylated CpGs within the Myog promoter (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Nuclear FAK de-represses Myog.
source: In other words, nuclear FAK de-represses Myog.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work (Luo et al., 2009).

claim: Caspase-mediated NPC trimming impairs FAK export from the nucleus during myogenic differentiation.
source: We here show that caspase-mediated NPC trimming impairs its export from the nucleus during myogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the nuclear accumulation of FAK shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The loss of MBD2-genome binding occurs within 24 hr as FAK becomes nuclear and precedes the degradation of MBD2 protein itself during myogenesis.
source: In line with this model, we find that the loss of MBD2-genome binding occurs within 24 hr as FAK becomes nuclear and precedes the degradation of MBD2 protein itself during myogenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CUT&RUN and immunoblotting shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: In mechanically stressed cells, focal adhesion proteins quickly translocate to the nucleus to function as transcription co-factors and induce rapid gene expression changes necessary for stress resolution.
source: Of note, in mechanically stressed cells, it is well-established that focal adhesion proteins quickly translocate to the nucleus to function as transcription co-factors and induce rapid gene expression changes necessary for stress resolution (Hervy et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: The mechanism of focal adhesion protein nuclear translocation in mechanically stressed cells may have been adapted for cell differentiation.
source: It is possible that this modus operandi has been adapted for cell differentiation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarity between mechanical stress response and differentiation.

claim: Diverse classes of proteins linked to DNA damage response accumulate in the nucleus during myogenesis, such as Annexin A2, E3 ligases (Itch and Ufl1), and proteasome subunits (Psmb3).
source: In addition, we find in the nucleus diverse classes of proteins that have been linked to DNA damage response, such as Annexin A2, E3 ligases (Itch and Ufl1), and proteasome subunits (Psmb3) (Chang et al., 2019; Jacquemont and Taniguchi, 2007; Madureira et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is observed in the mass spectrometry data and stated based on prior work linking these proteins to DNA damage response.

claim: DNA damage/repair is required for myogenesis.
source: This is in line with the fact that DNA damage/repair is required for myogenesis (Al-Khalaf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Multiple mitochondrial proteins enter the nucleus during myogenesis, hinting that nuclear-mitochondrial communication plays a role in myogenic differentiation.
source: Multiple mitochondrial proteins enter the nucleus as well, hinting that nuclear-mitochondrial communication plays a role myogenic differentiation (Soledad et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data and stated based on prior work.

claim: NPC trimming might be an NPC-genome interaction reset mechanism.
source: NPC trimming might also be anNPC-genome interaction reset mechanism.
evidence: This is speculated based on known roles of NPC-genome interactions.

claim: NPC-genome interaction is cell type-specific.
source: It is well established that NPC-genome interaction (1) is cell type-specific, (2) is reconfigured during differentiation, and (3) regulates cell identity genes (Cho and Hetzer, 2020; Ibarra et al., 2016; Jacinto et al., 2015; Labade et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: NPC-genome interaction is reconfigured during differentiation.
source: It is well established that NPC-genome interaction (1) is cell type-specific, (2) is reconfigured during differentiation, and (3) regulates cell identity genes (Cho and Hetzer, 2020; Ibarra et al., 2016; Jacinto et al., 2015; Labade et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: NPC-genome interaction regulates cell identity genes.
source: It is well established that NPC-genome interaction (1) is cell type-specific, (2) is reconfigured during differentiation, and (3) regulates cell identity genes (Cho and Hetzer, 2020; Ibarra et al., 2016; Jacinto et al., 2015; Labade et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Transient proteolysis of the nuclear basket can be an elegant reinitialization mechanism for NPC-genome interactions.
source: Transient proteolysis of the nuclear basket can be an elegant reinitialization mechanism.
evidence: This is speculated based on the role of the nuclear basket in NPC-genome interactions.

claim: In the context of acute ER stress, NPC trimming might be a stress-coping mechanism that curtails mRNA export and reduces the protein synthesis/folding load.
source: In the context of acute ER stress, NPC trimming might be a stress-comping mechanism that curtails mRNA export and reduces the protein synthesis/folding load.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of NPC trimming during ER stress.

claim: If ER stress becomes chronic and caspases linger for a prolonged period, it can jeopardize cellular homeostasis as nuclear levels of NES-containing proteins will remain abnormally high.
source: However, if ER stress becomes chronic and caspases linger for a prolonged period, it can jeopardize cellular homeostasis as nuclear levels of NES-containing proteins will remain abnormally high.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of persistent NPC trimming during chronic ER stress.

claim: Exhaustive NPC disintegration during apoptosis may simply be an extreme version of NPC trimming.
source: The present study establishes caspase-mediated NPC trimming as a key event in cell differentiation and stress response. It also points to the idea that exhaustive NPC disintegration during apoptosis may simply be an extreme version of this phenomenon.
evidence: This is speculated based on the comparison between NPC trimming and apoptotic NPC destruction.

claim: Some consider apoptosis as a radical form of caspase-mediated cellular transformation.
source: In fact, some consider apoptosis as a radical form of caspase-mediated cellular transformation (Burgon and Megeney, 2018; Connolly et al., 2014), and our results suggest that time is ripe to reassess the death-centric view of caspases.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: The results suggest that time is ripe to reassess the death-centric view of caspases.
source: In fact, some consider apoptosis as a radical form of caspase-mediated cellular transformation (Burgon and Megeney, 2018; Connolly et al., 2014), and our results suggest that time is ripe to reassess the death-centric view of caspases.
evidence: This is the authors' perspective based on their findings.

claim: SCH772984, an ERK1/2 inhibitor, accelerates survivin downregulation, caspase-3 activation, Nup153 degradation, and myogenin induction.
source: Consistently, we find that SCH772984, an ERK1/2 inhibitor, accelerates survivin downregulation, caspase-3 activation, Nup153 degradation, and myogenin induction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ERK1/2 inhibition stimulates myogenesis by promoting cell-cycle exit as well as cell-cell fusion.
source: ERK1/2 inhibition stimulates myogenesis by promoting cell-cycle exit as well as cell-cell fusion (Eigler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: When the nuclear translocation of NFAT was blocked by FK506, cells failed to upregulate myogenin but still activated caspase-3.
source: When the nuclear translocation of NFAT was blocked by FK506, a calcineurin inhibitor, cells failed to upregulate myogenin as previously reported (Armand et al., 2008) but still activated caspase-3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The calcineurin/NFAT pathway is orthogonal to the caspase-3 activation pathway.
source: This result illustrates that the calcineurin/NFAT pathway is orthogonal to the caspase-3 activation pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking NFAT does not prevent caspase-3 activation.

claim: DAPT, a γ-secretase inhibitor that blocks Notch intracellular domain release, neither affected myogenin upregulation nor caspase-3 activation.
source: Lastly, DAPT, a γ-secretase inhibitor that blocks Notch intracellular domain release, neither affected myogenin upregulation nor caspase-3 activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Pom121 was proteolyzed in a caspase-dependent manner during myogenesis.
source: For more comprehensive survey, we tested 8 additional scaffold Nups and 1 transmembrane Nup, Pom121, which is cleaved by caspase-3 in apoptotic cells (Figure 1B). Only Pom121 exhibited caspase-dependent proteolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Caspase-3-exposed NPCs will lack cytoplasmic filaments (Nup358 and Nup214), nuclear basket (Nup153 and Tpr), and the C-terminal tail of Pom121 that extends into the cytoplasm.
source: Given that caspase-3-exposed NPCs will lack cytoplasmic filaments (Nup358 and Nup214), nuclear basket (Nup153 and Tpr), and the C-terminal tail of Pom121 that extends into the cytoplasm, we termed this phenomenon "NPC trimming".
evidence: This is inferred from the identity of the Nups degraded during myogenesis.

claim: Since the NPC core is unaffected, functional NPCs can be quickly restored once caspases are quenched.
source: Importantly, since the NPC core is unaffected, functional NPCs can be quickly restored once caspases are quenched.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that scaffold Nups remain intact and Nup levels recover.

claim: The transcript levels of all but one Nups remain stable during myogenesis.
source: RNA-seq shows that the transcript levels of all but one Nups remain stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nup210 is the only Nup whose expression level changes dramatically during myotube formation at both transcript and protein levels.
source: Nup210 is the only exception whose expression level changes dramatically during myotube formation at both transcript and protein levels as we have previously reported (D'Angelo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work from the authors' lab and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
